claims.statement: scripts/ci-status.mjs derives two check states that the raw Forgejo API misreports rather than trusting the literal payload: a path-gated job reads status=success with description "Has been skipped" (fails safe, since the payload never states why), and a run cancelled by a newer push reads status=failure on every context it touched even though nothing broke (fails loud, announcing a broken build that isn't); classifyCheckState checks the cancelled description or the owning run's own cancelled status before the success/failure branches to catch this.

ci-status.mjs prints one of three skip-cause annotations derived by walking `needs:` edges parsed out of .forgejo/workflows/*.yml, because the commit-status payload for a skipped job never states why it was skipped: '(path-gated -> satisfied)' when every needs: dependency passed, '(NOT run - needs: X, which did not pass)' when a declared dependency failed, and '(skipped - cause not determined: ...)' when the workflow can't be parsed or the dependency hasn't reported yet.

app-ci's app-e2e job is gated behind a dorny paths-filter `changes` job scoped to paths that affect app runtime behaviour (a `app:` filter of frontend/**, agents/**, mcp-servers/**, backend/**, packages/**, infrastructure-as-code/docker/**, app-ci.yml itself, the zap scripts, the pnpm lockfile/workspace manifests, and a short list of NAMED scripts rather than `scripts/**`), so a PR touching only docs/, openwiki/, or a script the filter does not name renders app-e2e `skipped -> satisfied` and the board goes green without the E2E suite ever executing, making the suite's true failure rate invisible from an all-green streak.

cd-dispatch-gate.mjs (run by app-ci's advisory trigger-cd job) imports scripts/ci-status.mjs to reuse its cancelled/superseded/skipped classification, and that job runs node directly with no pnpm install step and no node_modules, so ci-status.mjs and every module it imports must stay dependency-free (node builtins and repo-local files only); a devDependency import such as the `yaml` package passes local tests but crashes trigger-cd on main with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and because trigger-cd is advisory this failure blocks nothing and posts no required-context signal.

ci-status.mjs classifies a commit-status context's event from Forgejo's `event` field (push/pull_request/etc, embedded as a suffix like `guardrails / secret-scan (push)`), while a scheduled (cron) run reports `event: push` even though the run's `trigger_event` field is `schedule`; a step gated `if: github.event_name == 'schedule'` follows trigger_event and does run on the cron, so reading the `event` field alone to decide whether a scheduled check ever executed produces a false conclusion that it never ran.

Because a branch-protection required-check glob like `guardrails*` or `app-ci / app-e2e*` matches a context regardless of its event suffix, ci-status.mjs separates the whole-commit verdict (which evaluates every context any required glob matches, across all events, the same way branch protection does) from the single-event view chosen by --pr/--event; a verdict that only looked at one event previously reported VERDICT mergeable for a commit whose required context had actually failed on a different event, and the subsequent merge call was rejected by the forge.

bundleJobName() in ci-status.mjs must derive the evidence-bundle-owning job differently depending on context shape: a real Actions check renders as `<workflow> / <job>` with spaces, where the job is the trailing segment, while a job's self-posted narrow status such as `infra-image-scan/weekly` carries no ` / ` separator and the bundle-owning job is the leading segment, not the trailing label; using tail-splitting uniformly on the narrow form produces a confident false '404, bundle not found' for a bundle that exists under the correct name.

ci-log-step.sh records one row per wrapped CI step into a per-run duration sample (step, seconds, exit code, ceiling) on every run, success or failure, and scripts/ci-step-ceilings.tsv is generated from that sample by `ci-status.mjs durations --propose` using the rule max(observed) x 3 (rounded up to a minute, floored at 300s); a step killed at its ceiling is recorded as censored and excluded from the sample specifically to prevent an anti-ratchet failure where each kill would shrink the next calibration's observed maximum and tighten the ceiling until legitimate runs start failing.

Only app-e2e publishes a counts bundle on an explicit green run: counts mode is self-limiting BY CONSTRUCTION because COUNTS_SOURCES names only step logs app-e2e produces, so every other green job finds no sources and reports `digest-outcome=not-needed` — leaving no bundle, no per-job log endpoint and no commit status for what its steps measured (measured on cd-deploy run 3430, where the job's success left no trace and the prod-apk disk measurement had only ever been readable because the job failed). The pattern used to recover a measurement from an otherwise-silent green job is to have the step export its value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and add an always()-gated, continue-on-error recorder that curls it onto the commit as its own commit status, with the state always 'success' and the finding carried in the description, values passed through raw including `<unset>`, and a context name verified against the live required-check glob list so it cannot accidentally start gating merges.

A pull request opened via an AGit push (HEAD:refs/for/main) has no backing branch — its head.ref is refs/pull/<n>/head — so Forgejo treats the run as untrusted and executes it without Actions secrets, silently emptying every ${{ secrets.* }} rather than failing the job outright; the resulting failure does not mention secrets (the empty NX_SELF_HOSTED_REMOTE_CACHE_ACCESS_TOKEN makes nx report a misconfigured remote cache endpoint), and the tell is measuring the secret's length inside the job — 0, sha256 e3b0c44298fc — versus 64 on a branch-backed PR. scripts/ci-status.mjs detects the non-branch head shape and prints a DETACHED HEAD warning for it, because the condition is invisible in the web UI; the warning is suppressed once the PR is closed or merged, since a deleted head branch reverts head.ref to the same ref and warning there would call a correctly-run green PR untrustworthy.

mc-service writes its domain-event log line at the end of a request handler, in the same emit as the response, so logs/mc-service.log's line order is completion order rather than start order: logging_middleware awaits next.run(request) and only then emits the `request completed` event carrying a numeric duration_ms, and handlers such as create_collection/delete_collection log their domain event after the command returns. Reconstructing true temporal (start) order for a bundle's mc-service log therefore requires subtracting each line's own duration_ms from its timestamp and sorting on that rather than trusting file order, and a cross-worker race hypothesis built from adjacent raw lines can be entirely inverted by this (item #568).

Cross-worker or cross-actor race hypotheses drawn from mc-service.log should be checked against `subject` / `preferred_username` / `authorized_party` before being accepted: authorized_party separates the actors even when every E2E worker acts as the same subject (movie-collection-manager = browser/BFF session, agent-gateway = the agent's downscoped write token) and preferred_username names the worker, while mc-service scopes collections by owner_id = token.subject in every collection endpoint, so two lines with different subject values cannot be acting on the same collection and a foreign worker's delete is impossible rather than a race to narrow.

There is no re-run endpoint in this forge build — measured 2026-08-31, actions/runs/{id}/rerun, actions/tasks/{id}/rerun and actions/runs/{id}/rerun-failed-jobs all answer 404 — so re-triggering a failed run means producing a new head sha (git commit --amend --no-edit plus a force-push re-fires the whole pull_request run), which must be budgeted as the full suite (~35 minutes of capacity-1 time) rather than the one job that failed.

The required-check globs are read live from GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branch_protections for the target's BASE branch rather than hand-maintained, because a hardcoded array drifted and over-reported mergeable (measured 2026-07-26: VERDICT mergeable and exit 0 for PR #103 while POST /pulls/103/merge answered 405 'Not all required status checks successful'). A fetch failure degrades rather than aborts but the header says so, and parseRequiredGlobs returns null — never an empty array — when no status-check rule covers the branch, because an empty required set would mark every context optional and render everything mergeable.

Query shape is a correctness rule for ci-status.mjs, not a performance tweak: ?head_sha=<full-sha> is a true server-side filter returning ~15 KB in 0.48 s, while ?limit=N alone, ?status=, ?event= and ?branch= are silently ignored and fall back to a ~12.4 MB / 94 s payload (~800x), and head_sha is exact-match so an abbreviated sha returns zero runs and reads as 'no CI ran'. A missing route and an empty result are different facts that both render as 'nothing there': /actions/runs/{id}/jobs answers with a non-JSON body so a naive pipe to jq dies on a parse error, /actions/workflows/<file>/runs is a real 404, and a padded 40-character sha returns [] plus an empty status object, indistinguishable from a commit with no checks.

ci-status.mjs distinguishes exit 0 (mergeable) / 1 (a required context genuinely failed) / 2 (bad arguments, missing token or scope) / 3 (watch timed out still waiting — runner starvation, not failure) / 4 (watch only: mergeable, but the dispatched cd-deploy run FAILED, item 823). Since item #403 watch waits for ADVISORY contexts by default because 'has this commit settled' is the question it is asked; --required-only narrows the wait back to the merge question, and an advisory context still running at the timeout does not change the exit code — exit 0 meaning mergeable is load-bearing for a `ci-status ... && merge` wrapper, so the unfinished advisory row is named instead of being silently dropped. An advisory FAILURE is announced in its own `⚠️ ADVISORY FAILURE` block placed immediately above the `VERDICT` line (because `VERDICT mergeable` is what actually gets read), naming each failed non-required context and what it cost; that block is rendered from the GATE rather than from the event-filtered view, so a push-only advisory failure such as `app-ci / trigger-cd` is still named while the view is scoped to `pull_request`. 4 is no verdict's code, so a caller can tell 'the deploy failed' from 'keep waiting' (3) and 'CI failed' (1).

--run N resolves the run's own commit and fetches its bundle (item #226, fixed 2026-09-01); before the fix the flag was parsed and read by no code path, so resolveSha fell through to git rev-parse HEAD and the tool answered confidently about the working copy ('No failed jobs on this commit'), a false negative rather than an error. The empty-result message now names the commit it examined so a wrong target is visible in the answer itself, and watch --branch main still reports on whatever main resolves to locally, which can be several merges stale.

A schedule-triggered run posts no <workflow> / <job> commit status at all, so `failure --run <id>` read contexts, found none, and answered 'No failed jobs on <sha> — checked every event's contexts' with exit 0 for a run whose own API status is failure (item #485, fixed 2026-09-19). The fix carries the run's own status through from the --run lookup, so the command now reports that the run FAILED but posted no commit status and exits 1; status carries the terminal verdict on this forge while conclusion is undefined on every run measured, and ?trigger_event=schedule is silently ignored so scheduled runs must be filtered client-side (or by ?workflow_id=<file> server-side).

A pending context is the absence of a commit status rendered as a state, not a promise that a job will run: it can still resolve to skipped (path-gated) or superseded, and actions/tasks does not disambiguate because a run queued but not yet dispatched has no task row at all. Absence in the capped, repo-wide 50-row actions/tasks window is not evidence a job was never scheduled, and a genuinely path-gated job does eventually post success with description 'Has been skipped', so a permanent waiting state means not-yet-evaluated — measured 2026-09-18 on PRs #479 and #482, whose statuses resolved on their own about seven minutes after a check declared them dead. The reliable check is the commit's own status history, which carries timestamps and is not a capped window.

cd-dispatch / trigger-cd is not a CI result: it is published by scripts/cd-dispatch-gate.mjs and is the only place a declined deploy is visible (before item #230 a run that declined to dispatch and a run that deployed looked identical from outside, and a merged commit went undeployed for a day — measured 2026-08-22 on PR #217). A superseded tip or 'nothing deployable changed since the last deploy' is published as success (a correct non-deploy), while a guardrails failure, an unfinished guardrails run or no guardrails at all is published as failure and also reds the job, so this status must be read before concluding a deploy was lost.

The forge scans the ENTIRE commit message for a CI-skip marker ([skip ci], [ci skip], [no ci], [skip actions], [actions skip]) and skips every workflow when it finds one, on push, pull_request and pull_request_sync alike — so a marker quoted in a body paragraph, bullet or code fence silently disables CI for that commit (measured 2026-08-31 on PR #322, where a commit body describing cd-deploy's promotion marker produced zero runs). The tell that separates it from a dead runner is that /actions/tasks still shows recent tasks for other branches, and the fix is to reword the message and force-push, never to disable the feature.

The two forge credentials have disjoint scopes and each fails in a way that reads as a different problem: MCM_FORGE_TOKEN is the read-only token (read:repository + read:issue + read:package) and answers 403 'token does not have at least one of required scope(s): [write:repository]' on POST /pulls, while the git credential fill credential is write-capable yet repository-scoped only — it returns 403 on issues/{n}/comments and 401 on the package registry, and an EMPTY package list rather than an error, which reads as 'no bundle was published' for a bundle that exists. So PR creation and workflow_dispatch use the write credential and packages must be read with MCM_FORGE_TOKEN; in a dev container the credential-helper proxy forwards the write credential over an IPC socket, and where it returns nothing the fallback is to push the branch and open the PR in the web UI, never AGit.

A merged branch is removed by the branch reaper, not by the merge: `default_delete_branch_after_merge: true` (enabled 2026-08-29, item #290) is the default for the web UI merge button ONLY, so an API merge that omits `delete_branch_after_merge: true` leaves the head branch behind (measured the same evening — PRs #287 and #293 passed the flag and their branches were gone, PR #291 omitted it and had to be cleaned up by hand), and that rule did not hold in the field: by 2026-10-30, 33 fully merged branches with no open PR had accumulated on origin back to 2026-09-26, and the four `renovate/lock-file-maintenance*` heads left by the API merges of PRs #832–#835 produced four empty, red PRs (#874–#877) because Renovate reuses a surviving branch's stale commit instead of regenerating. The backstop added by item #879 is `.forgejo/workflows/branch-reaper.yml`, which runs `scripts/reap-merged-branches.mjs --apply` on every push to main, on a daily 02:30 UTC cron and on `workflow_dispatch` — the cron sits ahead of Renovate's nightly 03:00 and its Friday window, so a stale `renovate/*` branch is gone before Renovate decides whether to reuse it. Still passing the flag is worth doing because it removes the branch at once, but it is now a convenience rather than the guarantee; an open PR's head and automation-owned branches such as `openwiki-maintenance` must not be deleted.

GET /pulls/{n} reports head.sha as the branch's CURRENT TIP, not the commit that was merged, so merged: true can co-exist with a head.sha that main does not contain — measured 2026-08-01 on PR #119, where head.sha was created 47 minutes after the merge, and again 2026-09-19 on PR #498, where head.sha and the merge commit's own parents disagreed and one of two commits silently did not ship. A PR's head.sha is therefore a claim about the branch and never about the merge; only git merge-base --is-ancestor plus the merge commit's parents (and a content check) are evidence.

An absence reported under a --job filter is a claim about the filter until it has been checked without one: measured 2026-08-30 on PR #289, `failure --pr 289 --job "infra-image-scan / infra-image-scan"` — the context form this tool prints in its own status table — reported 'no digest was published for them' while the digest was on the PR the whole time naming all five blocking findings, because the digest marker carries the BARE job name. Both halves are fixed (--job accepts either form, and a filter that excludes every digest now names what is available), but the durable protection is to drop the filter and look again before concluding a digest is absent.

A workflow_dispatch run posts no commit status, so ci-status status --sha keeps reporting 'waiting' regardless of the outcome — the per-job state has to be read from GET /actions/tasks instead, where Forgejo puts the outcome in `status` (running / success / failure / skipped) rather than in a GitHub-style status-plus-conclusion pair, and where `conclusion` is null even for successful tasks. The bundle id is not the run_number from that listing either: the bundle is named from GITHUB_RUN_ID (a repository-wide counter) while run_number is per-workflow, so constructing <run_number>--<job> returns 404 and reads as 'no bundle published' for a bundle that exists; list the package versions and take the newest for the job.

The deploy gate decides on the EFFECTIVE TIP of main, not on the commit that triggered it: cd-dispatch-gate.mjs computes the newest commit that will actually run a workflow (skipping commits carrying a `[skip ci]`-family marker, because cd-deploy's own promotion commit is pushed with one and would otherwise make the commit that legitimately owns the deploy look superseded), reports `superseded` as a non-fatal success when an older commit hands off, and only dispatches when guardrails are green on the tip. The dispatch sends `{"ref":"main"}` rather than the verified sha, so dispatching from a superseded commit would deploy a tree whose CI was never checked; the tip question is therefore answered BEFORE guardrails are read, because a superseded commit's guardrails legitimately report `failure`.

Membership in app-ci's `app` filter follows one stated rule rather than `scripts/**`: a script that DEPLOYS or CONFIGURES what app-e2e exercises belongs in the filter, while a script that only REPORTS on the run (ci-status, ci-failure-digest, the e2e tallies, ci-log-step) does not, because it cannot make the app wrong. The rule came from item #520, where scripts/agent-stack.mjs changed how the gateway receives its credentials and app-e2e — the only job that would have proven the gateway still starts — was skipped because nothing in the filter matched `scripts/**`; the guard test scripts/__tests__/app-ci-lockfile-filter.guard.test.mjs pins the wiring (including that `mobile` stays a strict subset of `app`) because this forge exposes no jobs/steps endpoint and a green tick cannot show which filter matched.

The deploy gate's decision is a pure function (`decide()`), tested against the item #230 incident's own payloads in scripts/__tests__/cd-dispatch-gate.test.mjs, and its workflow wiring is separately pinned by scripts/__tests__/app-ci-trigger-cd.guard.test.mjs — which asserts the checkout (fetch-depth: 0, so `git diff <last promotion commit>..HEAD` can resolve its base) precedes the gate step and that the dispatch step is conditional on the gate's `dispatch` output, because a pure function nothing calls is decoration and a shallow clone would silently disable the redundant-deploy skip on every run.

`shouldPublish` in ci-failure-digest.mjs is three-way and is checked in this order: a cancelled RUN publishes nothing at all (its contexts read `failure` for a commit that was never broken, so publishing would upsert noise on every rapid re-push), a job whose own status is `failure` publishes the full digest, and an EXPLICIT `success` publishes counts mode — while an unknown or missing status publishes nothing, deliberately, because a job that once lost CI_DIGEST_JOB_STATUS published a spurious digest on a green run and treating unknown as publishable-in-a-cheaper-mode would resurrect that bug.

A green app-e2e's counts bundle is small and deliberately narrow: it carries the `[e2e-gate]` counts (gate tier and model tier), the `[e2e-contention]` tally, the `[e2e-turn-tally]` verdict, the opt-in full mobile suite's per-flow table, and the `web-e2e` log reduced to its `[global-setup]`/`[playwright]` setup lines only — no PR comment, no health blocks, no container logs, and never a commit status. It needs the purpose-scoped CI_DIGEST_TOKEN because the package registry requires a scope the run-provisioned token lacks; without it the counts are still printed to the job log unconditionally, so the outcome is narrowed rather than lost, and the same counts path also runs bundle retention because publishing on every green run is what makes unbounded growth reachable.

On a green app-e2e the job judges its own counts rather than relying on someone reading the bundle: app-ci runs `node scripts/e2e-failure-set.mjs gate <web-e2e.log>` (and a separate non-blocking model-tier gate) which fails on `skipped > 0`, `did not run > 0` or a log with no summary at all — never re-failing on `failed > 0` — and runs `scripts/e2e-contention-tally.sh --gate`, which fails on `refresh_429 > 0` or `session_evicted > 0` but deliberately stays silent when the source is `unavailable`, since that implies bring-up already failed. Neither gate may carry `continue-on-error`: with it restored the step still runs and still prints its failure, so the log looks identical while the job passes regardless. The `flaky` count and the identities of the flaky tests reach no artifact on the green path except through this step's log, which is what the counts bundle publishes.

selectReapable() in scripts/reap-merged-branches.mjs deletes a branch only when every one of four conditions holds — its tip is an ancestor of origin/main, it heads no OPEN pull request, it is not exempt (main, openwiki-maintenance), and its tip commit is older than a 6 h grace period — and every uncertain answer is fail-closed: ancestry that cannot be answered keeps the branch, an unreadable tip date keeps it, and collectOpenPrHeads throws rather than returning fewer rows when a page errors or comes back short of its own x-total-count, because 'I could not read the open PRs' must never read as 'there are no open PRs'. The delete is leased to the exact sha that was classified via `git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<sha>` rather than the forge's DELETE /branches endpoint, which has no such precondition, so a commit pushed between classification and deletion is never destroyed; a bare invocation is a dry run and --apply is required; and unlike the comment-only jobs the workflow goes red on failure, because a reaper that silently stopped reaping is exactly the absence it exists to end.

The two forge credentials have disjoint roles and each failure reads as a different problem: MCM_FORGE_TOKEN is the READ side (read:repository + read:issue + read:package) and CI_DIGEST_TOKEN the WRITE side (write:issue + write:package + read:repository), stored as an Actions secret and deliberately not CD_PUSH_TOKEN — a whitelisted-user PAT able to push protected main, which spreading across ~20 jobs to publish diagnostics would expand into a real privilege escalation — nor the run-provisioned GITHUB_TOKEN, which cannot write issues or packages. Missing scopes fail loudly naming the scope, because a bare 401/403 is indistinguishable from an expired credential and cost this design a full revision cycle. Because CI_DIGEST_TOKEN is an Actions secret it is blank exactly when a run is most confusing (an AGit-headed push empties every secrets.* — the 2026-08-01 run collected its evidence, could not publish it, printed it to a job log the forge API cannot serve, and exited 0 with zero comments and no signal), so the digest falls back to the run-provisioned token, which can write a commit status `ci-digest/<job>` carrying the failing step name and a truncated excerpt; that path is recorded as `published` with `degraded: true` rather than `failed`, because `failed` means the evidence did not reach a channel and the reader's question is whether the diagnosis got through, and when both credentials are absent the outcome is `failed:no-credential`.

A pipe throws ci-status.mjs's exit code away — `ci-status … watch | tail -30` reports tail's status, so exit 3 (still waiting, runner starvation), exit 1 (a required context failed) and exit 4 (mergeable but the dispatched deploy failed) all arrive as 0. Measured 2026-09-06: a watch whose own output said `still waiting after 5100s … (exit 3)` was recorded by the session as WATCH_EXIT=0. The workaround is to redirect and read the file (`… watch --pr 372 --timeout 5100 > /tmp/watch.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"`), since `set -o pipefail` is not on by default in these sessions.

'Does this branch still contribute?' is a two-dot diff question, not a three-dot one: `git diff main...branch` reports what the branch adds since the merge base, so changes main already has by another route still appear as live work, while `git diff main branch` shows what the trees actually differ by. Measured on PR #262: three-dot said three version moves remained unique to the PR, two-dot showed merging it would have downgraded crates, and Renovate autoclosed it minutes later.

Two pieces of the branch-reaper workflow's wiring are silent-disable hazards rather than tidiness, and both are pinned by guard tests: the checkout takes `fetch-depth: 0`, because the reaper decides by `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<branch> origin/main` and a shallow single-ref clone cannot answer it — every branch would then read 'ancestry unanswerable' and nothing would ever be reaped; and the job is handed the run-provisioned `GITHUB_TOKEN` rather than `CD_PUSH_TOKEN`, because a deletion job has no business holding a whitelisted-user PAT that can push protected `main`.

The branch reaper reports a decision for every remote branch rather than only acting: each kept branch is printed with the reason it was kept ('exempt', 'head of an open PR', 'ancestry unanswerable', 'not merged into main', 'tip date unreadable', 'inside grace period') and each deletion with the sha it was classified at, so a run is auditable instead of merely applied. Its argument contract is deliberately narrow — near-miss spellings such as `--aply`, `-apply`, `--Apply`, `--dry-run` or `--force` are rejected with an ArgvError rather than silently read as either a dry run or an apply, a positional argument is rejected, and `--help` wins outright even beside `--apply`.

A dispatched cd-deploy run posts NO commit status for its outcome, so scripts/ci-status.mjs resolves the deploy from the runs listing it already fetches by head_sha (findDispatchedDeploy, item 823) and shows it as one ADVISORY row, `cd-deploy / build-deploy (dispatched)  <state>  run <id>`, plus a `🚨 DEPLOY FAILED (advisory)` block. The row is added after the lists the verdict is computed from and `required` is forced false, so no branch-protection glob can claim it and the verdict line and exit code are exactly what they were without it — the deploy runs after the merge it would be gating, which is why `status` keeps exit 0 ⟺ mergeable. A `cancelled` or `skipped` deploy is neither `passed` nor a failure, and the newest run by `id` wins so a re-run decides.

Two measured payload shapes silently defeat a deploy resolver written from the GitHub docs, because a match failure produces silence rather than an error: a dispatched run carries `event: ""` with the actual event in `trigger_event`, and it carries its sha in `commit_sha` rather than `head_sha`. The GitHub spellings are accepted too, so a payload that fills them still matches. The bundle is named by the run's `id`, never by `index_in_repo` (the number the UI shows), so a name built from the UI number 404s for a bundle that exists — run 5745 is "5744" in the UI and its bundle is `5745--build-deploy`.

When a sha has a failed dispatched cd-deploy run, `failure --sha` / `--run` prints the deploy's digest from the bundle `<runId>--build-deploy` or `<runId>--prod-apk` (every cd-deploy job that publishes a digest is tried quietly, since usually only one failed), and with neither published it prints `deploy run <id> FAILED; no evidence bundle published` and exits 1 — it never answers "No failed jobs". `watch` waits for a running deploy as for any advisory context and exits 4 when the commit is mergeable and the deploy failed, which no verdict produces.

The dispatched deploy runs on main's head AT DISPATCH TIME, which is not always the commit whose CI dispatched it, so a sha whose `trigger-cd` passed can legitimately carry no cd-deploy run: measured 2026-10-21, `trigger-cd` passed on 7cc3c304 while the deploy ran on fa79e611, a marker commit pushed in between. ci-status.mjs names that case explicitly — `no deploy dispatched for this sha — trigger-cd passed, but no cd-deploy run carries this sha` — and the remedy is to run `status` on the commits after it in `git log --first-parent main`, not to conclude the deploy was lost.

Item 823's case study is what the resolver exists for: on 2026-10-21 cd-deploy run 5745 (the UI calls it 5744) on fa79e611 failed at scan-push, `failure --sha` said `No failed jobs on fa79e611 — checked every event's contexts`, `failure --run 5745` said `posted NO commit status`, a session watching for the `chore(cd): promote` commit timed out, and the evidence existed all along as the bundle `5745--build-deploy`, read by hand. scripts/__tests__/ci-status.test.mjs pins the whole path against the real payloads in fixtures/ci-status/, and `ci-status --selftest` carries the case so the trap is classified without a forge.

`app-ci / app-image-scan` is a REQUIRED app-ci job that needs [changes, app-e2e], runs with `always()` (so a skipped app-e2e cannot cascade-skip it and a required context always posts) on the `kvm` runner against app-e2e's own rootless daemon socket, passes early in seconds when `changes.outputs.app` is not `true` (`no app path changed — images identical to main's`), fails closed when the `changes` job itself did not succeed (an unknown app diff must not read as nothing to scan), and verifies all six `app-scan/<name>:run-<run id>` tags exist before scanning any of them — so it never passes on images it could not find.

`app-e2e` tags each of the six app images `app-scan/<name>:run-<run id>` unconditionally and immediately after they are built (before the E2E steps, so a later failing step still leaves the scan its images), and `app-image-scan` removes those run tags at the end with `always()` while leaving the `:latest` images in place; the per-RUN tag is what stops a later run rebuilding `:latest` on the persistent daemon from changing what is scanned.

`trigger-cd` gained `app-image-scan` as a `needs:` dependency and requires its result to be exactly `success`, so a red scan on `main` blocks the CD dispatch as well as the merge; because the scan job is itself `always()` and posts `success` when there was legitimately nothing to scan, only a skipped or failed scan is prevented from reaching a deploy.

`scripts/cd/scan-app-image.sh` returns 0 (scanned, no un-allowlisted fixable Critical) / 10 SCANNER ERROR (the scanner could not complete, so nothing was assessed and no verdict is taken) / 11 BLOCKING FINDING (the verdict's table names the image and the CVE) / 2 usage; it takes the verdict from `check-infra-image-findings.mjs` only after a scan that completed, so a scanner that could not run is never reported as a vulnerability finding. Each caller maps 10 and 11 to its own message — what the operator does next differs between a PR and a deploy — and `scan-push.sh` runs the shared call inside its per-image loop BEFORE `docker push` and fails closed on any other exit code, because an image that was not scanned must never be pushed.

The PR-time scan and the deploy run ONE pipeline: both callers invoke `scripts/cd/scan-app-image.sh` and neither runs `trivy image`, `infra-image-scan.mjs` or `check-infra-image-findings.mjs` itself, so a PR and the deploy that follows it share one set of flags and one allowlist (`security/infra-images/allowlist.yaml`); the Trivy version is pinned separately in each workflow that installs it (app-ci.yml, cd-deploy.yml, infra-image-scan.yml) and `renovate-workflow.guard.test.mjs` fails if those pins disagree or are not both pinned and agreeing with the version-tagged install script, while a drift guard in `scripts/__tests__/app-image-scan.test.mjs` fails if either caller starts scanning on its own or if the PR's image list and `scan-push.sh`'s image map disagree.

The residual after spec 084 US3 is real: a green PR can still meet a red deploy, because the vulnerability database moves between the PR's scan and the deploy's and because cd-deploy rebuilds the images (its `mcm-bff` bakes the public Keycloak host into the web bundle, though packages and base image are the same). That is why the job also runs on pushes to `main` so a database change reds before any dispatch, and why `scan-push` stays in place, unchanged in position, as the gate on what is actually pushed.

An allowlist entry suppresses a finding in the PR scan and the deploy gate at once, because both read the same `security/infra-images/allowlist.yaml`; entries must be keyed to the image DIGEST (`^<image>:<tag>@sha256:<prefix>`) so that a rebuild is scanned unsuppressed, and an entry carries a justification, an author and usually an expiry after which it stops suppressing.

The fifth measured quirk of `GET /actions/runs` is that a queued run's `started` is the EPOCH, not `null`: a run with `status: waiting` reports `started: "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"`, so the obvious narrowing filter (`select(.started > "<recent>")`) silently drops every queued run and reads exactly like `the push triggered nothing` (three runs created for one push were all invisible). Filter on `status` or `id` and read `started` only once the run has begun; a SORT by `Date.parse(started)` is safe because a queued run sorts oldest, but a FILTER on it is not.

The built-in fallback required-check list carries a seventh glob, `app-ci / app-image-scan*` (spec 084 US3), and the fallback is a SUBSET of live branch protection by design — it may lag, but an extra glob would mark a check required that is not and block a mergeable PR, so a guard test asserts every fallback glob is present in the branch-protection payload.

`scripts/cd/scan-app-image.sh` is listed in app-ci's `app` path filter (spec 084 US3) so that changing the shared scanner re-runs the job that calls it, and the same filter decides whether `app-image-scan` has anything to scan at all: a PR touching no app path makes the scan pass in seconds with `no app path changed`, which is a legitimate pass rather than a scan that found nothing.

Every `app-image-scan` step is on the `CI_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` backstop today — listed by name in `scripts/ci-step-ceilings.tsv`'s `ON THE BACKSTOP` block with no observations yet — and the job bounds them with its own `CI_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: '900'` below its 30-minute job ceiling, so a hung scan fails its step and the failure digest still runs.

The separator-less self-posted context form (`infra-image-scan/weekly`, `renovate/mode`) is safe to post only because branch protection requires the SPACED glob (`infra-image-scan / infra-image-scan*`) and a context with no ` / ` cannot match it — which is also why the head, not the tail, owns the bundle; and because a bundle that appears absent is often merely mis-named, the package registry should be listed (`GET /api/v1/packages/{owner}?type=generic&q=ci-failures`) before concluding no bundle exists.

The container registry is a third scope behaviour on the same forge, and the Docker CLI hides it in the direction that reads as a publish failure: `docker manifest inspect <forge registry>/<owner>/<image>:<sha>` answers `no such manifest` — NOT `unauthorized` — when the CLI is not logged in, so it reads as "this image was never published" for an image that exists (measured 2026-08-22, on a tag whose image was already pulled and listed in local `docker images`). The instrument is therefore unauthenticated and has said nothing about the tag in question. The rules that follow are: always run the control first by inspecting a tag known to exist, probe the registry API with `curl` against `/v2/<owner>/<image>/manifests/<sha>` instead, and use the read token `MCM_FORGE_TOKEN` there, because the `git credential fill` credential returns 401 on the registry (alongside its 403 on `issues/{n}/comments` and its empty package list).

A digest pinned from this registry request is the only trustworthy source for pinning an image: the packages API's newest row for a build is the provenance **attestation** (the `unknown/unknown` entry in the OCI index), and pinning it fails at pull time, while `manifests/<tag>` returns the index under every `Accept` header. Walking index → platform manifest → config blob and reading `history[].created_by` proves what is inside a published image without pulling it, and doubles as the check that an image did not accidentally end as `USER root`.

Package-registry retention (spec 084 US5) is `scripts/registry-retention.mjs`, configured by `infrastructure-as-code/forgejo/registry-retention.yaml` and run weekly by `.forgejo/workflows/registry-retention.yml` (Sundays 06:00 UTC, after the Friday Renovate window and outside the nightly backup). It is the only thing in this repository that deletes a **container image** version from the forge registry — the generic packages prune themselves at publish time — and the forge's own name-regex cleanup rules are deliberately unused because they cannot protect a digest a git file names, they live only in the web UI, and they have no report-only run.

Registry retention is report-only by default and a delete requires two independent keys held in two places: `--apply` is passed only by a `workflow_dispatch` whose `apply` input is true, and the script refuses it with exit 2 (naming the mismatch) unless the committed config also says `mode: apply` — so the schedule can never delete, and the path to deleting is report → review → a one-line PR flipping `mode: report` to `mode: apply` that links the reviewed report → a dispatch with `apply: true`. A bare local invocation reports, and `--json` / `--package <name>` narrow the report without changing the mode.

Retention decides each version by its FIRST applicable keep reason, else deletes it, and the ordering differs between the two kinds of version a push creates: a **tag** (the index, i.e. the head) is judged `keep:protected`, then `keep:newest` (among the newest `keepNewest` tags), then `keep:recent` (younger than `keepDays`), while a **`sha256:` child** is judged `keep:protected`, then `keep:referenced` (a KEPT index points at it, whatever its age), then `keep:unverified` (some kept index could not be read), then `keep:recent`, and only then deleted. Packages with unrebuildable artefacts use `keep:all`, and a package absent from the config is `keep:unconfigured` — reported, never deleted.

Children are kept by reference rather than by age, because an unchanged image REUSES the previous push's platform manifest: one push creates the tag `<sha>`, whose `manifest.json` is the digest a `.env.deploy` pins (an OCI image INDEX), plus the `sha256:` children that index references (the platform manifest, which owns the layers, and an attestation), so a child can be older than the newest tag that needs it — measured 2026-10-31 on `mc-service`, where the 07:48 deployed index pointed at a platform manifest created at 03:14 by an earlier push. "Delete what is old" would therefore delete the layers of the running image. If any kept index cannot be read, no child of that package is deleted at all (`keep:unverified`), and a child younger than `keepDays` is also kept as possibly a push in progress.

Every protection is computed from git BEFORE the first API call, and a shallow clone is REFUSED rather than protecting only HEAD (`fetch-depth: 0` in the workflow is load-bearing for that reason): `protectedDigests` reads the digest lines out of every `infrastructure-as-code/docker/*/.env.deploy` at the newest promotion and the 5 commits before it, so the protected set is the deployed images plus the rollback targets (a rollback being a `git revert` of a promotion). A shallow checkout would read as "nothing but HEAD to protect", a protection set that is silently too small.

Registry retention has a preflight that can only stop it: if a protected digest cannot be resolved to a registry version of a configured, listed package, the script exits 5 and deletes nothing, naming the digest and the `.env.deploy` it is pinned in — a real alarm meaning a deployed or rollback image is gone or the pin is wrong. When it does delete, indexes are deleted before children, so no index surviving a partial run points at a child that has already been removed.

The retention config is validated rather than half-read — an unknown top-level or per-package key, a duplicate package, a `mode` other than `report`/`apply`, `keepAll` combined with a window, a package that keeps nothing by rule, or a `ci-failures` window below `evidenceWindowDays` is refused naming the key — because a config that is silently half-parsed keeps less than its author believes. It also enforces the floor `ci-status durations` needs on the `ci-failures` bundles (`DEFAULT_DURATION_RUNS` × the number of bundle-publishing jobs, counted from the workflows themselves), so a newly added job that publishes a bundle fails the config until the floor is raised; the bundle publisher `ci-failure-digest.mjs` already prunes those at 30 days, so this rule is a backstop rather than the deleter.

The retention sweep authenticates with its own `REGISTRY_CLEANUP_TOKEN`, scoped `write:package` only and stored as an Actions secret, deliberately separate from the CI push token (`actions-ci-push`) so that rotating either cannot break the other; a report can also run with the read-only `MCM_FORGE_TOKEN`, and `MCM_FORGE_URL` has no default, so a missing URL or token is a usage error rather than a guess at a host.

The three-way Trivy pin is maintained rather than left to rot: a single `aquasecurity/trivy` regex customManager in `renovate.json` declares `managerFilePatterns` for all three installing workflows (`infra-image-scan.yml`, `cd-deploy.yml`, `app-ci.yml`) with datasource `github-releases` and `matchStrings: ["TRIVY_VERSION=(?<currentValue>v[\\d.]+)"]`, and `renovate-workflow.guard.test.mjs` asserts that manager exists exactly once, covers each of the three files, and that its matchStrings actually capture a currentValue in each — because a manager whose regex misses is indistinguishable from no manager at all.

Registry retention's report-only gate is still in force after the mode flip: the weekly schedule passes no `--apply` (RETENTION_ARGS is empty unless a dispatch sets `apply: true`), so the schedule can never delete regardless of the committed mode, and `registry-retention.mjs` refuses `--apply` with exit 2 naming the mismatch unless the config says `mode: apply`. The committed config has said `mode: apply` since the first report was reviewed (run 6350, item #863), so today a dispatch with `apply: true` is what deletes while the weekly run only reports — the two guards, not the mode value, are what the delete path rests on.

The forge's GENERIC package registry has no scheduled sweep — each publisher prunes opportunistically at publish time, which is why registry retention owns only the container images. `scripts/ci-failure-digest.mjs` deletes `ci-failures` bundle versions past its own 30-day `RETENTION_DAYS` (`selectExpiredVersions`, which KEEPS a version whose `created_at` will not parse, because deleting evidence on a parse failure is the destructive direction), and `scripts/cd/publish-apk.mjs` — invoked by `cd-deploy`'s `prod-apk` step on every deploy — keeps the newest **5** `mcm-app-android` versions by `created_at` plus any version whose name ends in `-keep`, which is never pruned and does not consume one of the 5 slots. That retention is COUNT-based rather than a day window because a quiet month would otherwise delete every installable APK, and a prune failure in either publisher is logged and swallowed rather than allowed to red a deploy.

Workflows in this repository cannot use `actions/upload-artifact` v4 or later: this forge's runner refuses any server other than github.com before it uploads anything (`GHESNotSupportedError`), a fact measured four times and most recently on both runner labels on 2026-10-16 (spec 081 research T004), so the action stays on v3 under a Renovate `allowedVersions` ceiling (item #912) and a Forgejo release note claiming support does not lift it. This is one of the reasons CI pushes its evidence digest into a channel the forge API can read rather than to an artifact, since there is no log, artifact or per-run-jobs endpoint to fetch it from either.

The `app-scan/<name>:run-<run id>` tags must be HELD by a container between `app-e2e` and `app-image-scan`, because on this single runner another run's `app-e2e`, `dast` or `build-deploy` can take the daemon in between and each begins with `docker image prune -af`, which deletes a bare tag (measured on PR #909, where `missing scan tag(s)` failed twice on images nobody had scanned after its own `app-e2e` had passed). `app-e2e` therefore holds each tag with a stopped container named `app-scan-hold-<run id>-<image>` and labelled `mcm.app-scan-hold`, which `image prune -a` never removes; `app-image-scan` removes its holds before its tags under `always()` (an `image rm` of a held tag only untags it), the hold is `rm -f`'d before being created because a re-run attempt keeps the same run id, and every one of the three image-prune sites first runs `docker container prune -f --filter label=mcm.app-scan-hold --filter until=24h` so a cancelled run's images are released after at most a day while a run still waiting for its scan keeps them. `docker ps -a --filter label=mcm.app-scan-hold` lists the holds, and holds from runs finished more than a day ago mean a prune site lost its sweep; `scripts/__tests__/app-image-scan.test.mjs` pins the sweep's label and age filters, their ordering before the image prune at all three sites, the site count, and that the hold is removed before the tag.

Matching a commit-status context to the run that produced it must key on the workflow file AND the run's trigger (`trigger_event || event`), never on `event` alone, because the same workflow runs several times on one sha and a cron run misreports `event: push`: measured 2026-11-01 on `7d27f72f`, the Friday cron (6172) and a push run (6164) of `infra-image-scan.yml` shared the sha, and the `event`-keyed match handed the push-suffixed check `infra-image-scan / infra-image-scan (push)` the CRON's run id — which is the id `failure --full` derives the evidence bundle from and the run whose `cancelled` status `classifyCheckState` reads, so the wrong id means a wrong bundle and a wrong superseded/failed call. A narrow, separator-less status carries no `(event)` suffix, so the events that post it cannot be read off the context and are declared in `NARROW_STATUS_EVENTS`, derived from each posting step's `if:`: `infra-image-scan/weekly` is `schedule` only, `renovate/mode` is `workflow_dispatch` only, and `infra-image-scan/expiry` and `cd-deploy/prod-apk-disk` post on every event except `pull_request`. An unlisted one falls back to 'the first run of that workflow on the sha', which is right only by list order, so a guard test fails when a workflow posts a separator-less status the table does not declare.
